title: How many kinds of fungi?
teaches: About 150,000 kinds named against 2 to 4 million estimated, how that estimate is made, and where the unnamed fungi are
summary: **About 150,000 kinds of fungi have been named.** A few thousand more are named each year, so naming the rest would take centuries at today's pace.
**The total is estimated by scaling up ratios.** Britain and Ireland have about six kinds of fungi for every native plant, which applied to the world's plants suggests well over a million.
**The best estimate is 2.2 to 3.8 million.** Soil DNA suggests that even this may be low.
**Most unnamed fungi are small and hidden.** They live in soil, inside leaves, on insects and in the tropics, and many are already in collections.

blocks.text: The world's fungi have been named one at a time since Linnaeus, each with a description and a specimen kept in a fungarium.[^fungarium] The total stands at about 150,000 kinds, and grows by a few thousand a year. That is fewer than the named beetles. Yet almost every mycologist believes that most fungi are still unnamed, and the question is by how much.

blocks.caption: The kinds of fungi named so far, against an estimate from the ratio of fungi to plants, and how long naming the rest would take.

blocks.text: In 1991 David Hawksworth, a mycologist and lichen specialist, made the first careful estimate. Britain and Ireland are unusually well studied: generations of amateurs and professionals have recorded their fungi for two hundred years. There, the known kinds of fungi outnumber the native vascular plants by about six to one. If the world had the same ratio, it would hold about 1.5 million kinds of fungi, roughly twenty times the number then named.[^ratio]

The method has obvious weak spots. The tropics have far more plants than Britain, and may have a different ratio. Many fungi live on insects or in soil and have no link to any one plant. In 2017 Hawksworth and Robert Lücking revised the figure using several lines of evidence and put it at between 2.2 and 3.8 million. By that estimate, between one kind in fifteen and one in twenty-five has a name.

The DNA surveys of the last lesson give another route. If a spoonful of forest soil holds hundreds of kinds, and soils a few kilometres apart share only some of them, the total across the world must be very large. Estimates built this way have come out higher, five million or more, though they depend on the grouping rules of the last lesson, which can split one species into several groups. The figures disagree, but none of them comes anywhere near the number already named.

The unnamed fungi are not mushrooms on a woodland path. Most are small or invisible. Inside the leaves of nearly every plant live fungi called endophytes, which do no visible harm; a single tropical tree can host dozens, many found nowhere else. Tiny fungi grow on the bodies of beetles and flies, each kind often tied to one kind of insect.[^laboulbeniales] Others live in the guts of animals, in lakes and in the deep sea, and many in soil grow only as threads and never fruit.

Some are already in hand. Fungarium drawers hold specimens collected decades ago that no one has had time to study, and Hawksworth and Lücking argued that a large share of the new species of the coming decades will be found there rather than in the field. Others are being found by amateurs. Naturalists posting photographs and specimens to sites such as iNaturalist, and community projects that barcode the mushrooms they collect, now add records of fungi faster than professionals alone could.[^amateurs]

A name is how knowledge is kept. Without one, a fungus that feeds the roots of a rare orchid or makes an antibiotic cannot be recorded, protected or looked up. Almost no fungi are on lists of threatened species, mainly because so few have been studied enough to assess. At a few thousand a year, naming the rest would take centuries, and some will disappear with their habitats first. The course has followed the fungi that are known; most of the kingdom is still to be met.

blocks.caption: Four questions on counting fungi
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: About how many kinds of fungi have been named?
How did Hawksworth make his 1991 estimate?
choices: He scaled up the British Isles' ratio of fungi to plants to the world's plants
He counted every fungus in a forest
He sequenced soil from every continent
items.why: Britain and Ireland have about six fungi for each native plant, so the world might too.

items.ask: Why might the ratio method give too low an answer?
choices: Many fungi live in soil or on insects, with no tie to one plant
Fungi are easier to see than plants
items.why: Fungi not tied to plants are left out, and the tropics may differ.

items.ask: In the figure, what does a faster naming rate do?
choices: Shortens the time to name the rest, though it is still centuries
Raises the estimate of how many kinds there are
items.why: Even at several thousand a year, naming millions takes hundreds of years.

ratio.title: The British and Irish numbers
ratio.text: Around 1990 Britain and Ireland had about 12,000 recorded kinds of fungi, lichens included, and about 2,000 native vascular plants. Hawksworth multiplied the world's then estimated 270,000 kinds of vascular plant by six and rounded down to 1.5 million.

amateurs.title: Barcodes from amateurs
amateurs.text: In North America, mushroom societies have sent tens of thousands of dried specimens for DNA barcoding through community projects, and some of them have turned out to be species new to science.

fungarium.title: Herbarium or fungarium
fungarium.text: Collections of dried fungi were long kept inside botanical herbaria, from the days when fungi were classed as plants. Many institutions, including Kew, now call their fungal collections fungaria.

laboulbeniales.title: Fungi on one leg of one beetle
laboulbeniales.text: Many of the insect-riding fungi belong to the Laboulbeniales, which look like tiny brushes sticking out of the shell. Some are so fussy that they grow only on one sex of one species of beetle, or only on the left rear leg, where the two beetles touch during mating.
